title: Never Photograph or Digitize the Word List
plain:
The fastest way to lose inherited bitcoin is to put the words somewhere phones, clouds, and malware can reach. Never photograph the word list or store it in a phone, cloud note, or email.

Many phones upload new photos to a cloud gallery automatically; an email or cloud note is one password reset away from a stranger; and malware on a device can read notes, files, and images at rest. A photo also carries time and place details you never meant to share.

The words belong on physical media you control - paper to start, metal for the long term - and nowhere else. If a photo or digital copy already exists, treat the words as exposed and plan, once you are comfortable, to move the funds to a fresh wallet.
technical: Digitizing a recovery phrase multiplies exposure paths: camera rolls on common phones auto-sync to cloud photo services, cloud notes and email are high-value accounts reachable through password resets and account-recovery attacks, and commodity malware routinely scans files, screenshots, and images for BIP-39 wordlists, with OCR making photographs of a phrase just as readable as text. Deleting a photo or note is unreliable remediation, because cloud trash, caches, and backups can retain copies indefinitely. If a phrase has ever been digitized, the conservative treatment is to consider it compromised: generate a new wallet on verified hardware, move the funds once the inheritor is ready, and retire the old phrase. The corpus baseline applies everywhere: record the recovery phrase offline on paper or metal, and never type it into a website, app, or chat. No specific vendor or product is implied.

warnings: Do not photograph, screenshot, or scan the word list, even briefly.
Do not store the words in a phone note, cloud document, email draft, or password manager.
Do not send the words through chat or messaging, not even to yourself.
Do not assume deleting a photo removes it from cloud backups or device caches.
